specAnchors.text: use the principle of conservation of energy

primer.text: Energy is the strictest accountant in physics: nothing created, nothing destroyed, everything transferred. This note states the principle, then walks it through a bat-and-ball strike, a boiling kettle and a trampoline cycle — watching useful and wasted branches close every account.

modules.title: The principle of conservation of energy
sourceHeadings: What is the principle of conservation of energy?
Examples of the principle of conservation of energy
modules.opening: One law underpins every energy account in physics: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores. A closed system keeps a constant total; whatever one system gains, another loses; and energy that spreads to the surroundings is never lost — merely no longer useful.
keyPoints: Energy is never created nor destroyed — it only moves between stores.
The total energy of a closed system remains constant.
Whatever one system gains, another system loses by the same amount.
Energy spreads out into the surroundings by heating and radiation — dissipated, and usually wasted.
Dissipated transfers are usually not useful, so the energy is described as wasted.

low.restatement: The books always balance: no transfer creates or destroys energy, closed systems keep their total, and the only place energy seems to vanish is into useless, dissipated spreading to the surroundings.
low.analogy: A sealed bag of marbles: you can pour them between pockets forever, but the bag’s count never changes.
low.examPointer: Use the exact statement in explain questions: cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another.

medium.restatement: Every gain is matched by an equal loss somewhere else; dissipation by heating and radiation spreads energy thinly through the surroundings, which is why it stops being useful without ever stopping to exist.
medium.analogy: A cup of tea cooling in a big cold room: the tea’s loss is the room’s gain, spread so thinly that no one can make a useful engine from it.
medium.examPointer: Wasted does not mean destroyed — say dissipated to the surroundings to keep the conservation law intact in your wording.

modules.title: Conservation in the bat-and-ball and kettle examples
sourceHeadings: Example 1: a bat hitting a ball
Example 2: Boiling Water in a Kettle
modules.opening: Two everyday scenes carry the law through every store and pathway. A bat strikes a ball: kinetic energy splits into the ball’s motion, wasted thermal bumps and dissipated sound and heat. A kettle boils: electrical energy lands in the element, flows into the water, and leaks wastefully into the plastic and the air.
keyPoints: The moving bat holds energy in its kinetic store.
Some of the bat’s kinetic energy transfers usefully to the ball’s kinetic store.
Some transfers mechanically to the ball’s thermal store on impact, and some dissipates by heating to the bat, ball and surroundings — both wasted.
In the kettle, energy is transferred electrically from the mains to the element’s thermal store.
The element transfers energy by heating to the water (useful) and to the plastic kettle body and surroundings (wasted).

low.restatement: Bat-and-ball: kinetic store splits into useful kinetic of the ball plus wasted thermal and radiated sound. Kettle: electrical input lands in the element, flows by heating into the water, and the plastic and air take the wasted share.
low.analogy: A fruit tree shaken by a shake-and-catch harvester: some fruit lands in the basket (useful), some bruises on the ground (wasted) — but no fruit is created or destroyed.
low.examPointer: Name the pathway at each link: mechanically on impact, electrically from the mains, by heating into the water.

medium.restatement: Both examples close the same loop: the input store empties, useful and wasted branches fill, and the surroundings receive the dissipated remainder — every joule accounted for.
medium.analogy: Splitting a pizza: the slices go to guests (useful), crumbs to the floor (wasted), but the pizza’s total never changes.
medium.examPointer: Questions often ask for ONE wasted transfer — the plastic kettle body and the sound of the strike are the classic answers.

modules.title: Conservation on the trampoline
modules.opening: A trampoline bounces the conservation law through four stores in one motion: gravitational store empties into kinetic on the way down, kinetic fills the elastic store as the canvas stretches, and the sequence reverses on the way up — shrinking a little each bounce as heating and sound take their share.
keyPoints: Falling: the jumper’s gravitational store transfers to the kinetic store.
At the canvas: kinetic transfers to the elastic store as the canvas stretches.
Rebounding: the elastic store returns energy to kinetic, then to gravitational as the jumper rises.
Each cycle transfers some energy to thermal stores and to sound, so the bounces shrink.
The jumper must supply fresh energy mechanically to keep bouncing at the same height.

low.restatement: The trampoline cycle is gravitational → kinetic → elastic → kinetic → gravitational, with thermal and sound skimming a little off every pass — the shrinking bounce is conservation made visible.
low.analogy: Water sloshing between four buckets through a leaky pipe: the water shuttles forever, but a few drops spill on every trip.
low.examPointer: Order the stores correctly for the phase asked: descending is gravitational to kinetic; stretched canvas is elastic.

medium.restatement: At every exchange some energy takes the heating or sound exit, so the maximum height falls unless the jumper’s muscles do mechanical work to refill the account.
medium.analogy: A payment where every transfer charges a small fee: the balance still exists but the useful balance shrinks each round trip.
medium.examPointer: If asked why the jumper keeps bouncing lower, name BOTH wasted routes: heating of the canvas and body, and sound.

glossary.definition: The principle that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another.
A system that exchanges no energy with its surroundings, so its total energy stays constant.
Spread out to the surroundings, usually by heating and radiation, so the energy is no longer useful.
Energy transferred to stores that do not serve the intended purpose.
The energy store of stretched, squashed or bent objects.
